subject: Coffee & Tea
title: CO₂ and Degassing
description: Learn CO₂ and Degassing in one minute.

hook.text: Freshly roasted coffee releases CO₂ for days. That gas is both friend and enemy of great coffee.

buildup.text: Roasting produces CO₂ trapped inside the bean's cellular structure. It escapes slowly after roasting.

discovery.text: Too much CO₂ repels water during brewing, causing uneven extraction. That's why fresh beans need rest.

twist.text: Most specialty roasters recommend waiting 3–7 days after roasting before brewing for optimal flavor.

climax.text: After about three weeks, most CO₂ is gone. Staling begins as oxygen takes over. The clock is ticking.

punchline.text: Too fresh is chaotic. Too old is flat. The sweet spot is brief.

quiz.question: Why should you wait a few days before brewing freshly roasted coffee?
options: Excess CO₂ repels water and causes uneven extraction

details.summary: Roasting generates CO2 trapped inside the bean's cell structure. Freshly roasted coffee releases this gas over days in a process called degassing. Too much CO2 repels water during brewing, causing uneven extraction. Most coffees reach their flavor peak 7 to 14 days after roasting.
details.whyItMatters: Degassing explains why freshly roasted coffee is not always best immediately. Knowing the timeline helps you brew each bag at its peak flavor window.
takeaways: Roasting traps CO2 inside the bean's cell structure
Peak flavor typically occurs 7 to 14 days after roasting
Excess CO2 prevents water from contacting grounds evenly

faq.question: Why does fresh coffee bloom so dramatically?
faq.answer: The bloom during pour-over is caused by CO2 escaping when hot water contacts fresh grounds. Freshly roasted coffee has more trapped gas, so the bloom is larger with visible bubbling. Stale coffee barely blooms because the CO2 has already escaped.

faq.question: Can you brew coffee the same day it is roasted?
faq.answer: You can, but results are often erratic because of excessive CO2. Espresso is especially affected since gas creates channeling. Waiting at least 3 to 5 days for filter coffee and 7 to 10 days for espresso gives more consistent extraction.
